options.text: The time the insurer has to contest statements on the application
The maximum length of time benefits will be paid
The time before a pre-existing condition is covered
The time after disability starts before benefits begin

explanation: The elimination period is like a time deductible: the number of days after the disability begins before benefits start. Longer elimination periods lower the premium.

distractorExplanations.a: Contesting misstatements falls under the time limit on certain defenses.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the benefit period, here 5 years.
distractorExplanations.c: That is a pre-existing condition waiting period, not the elimination period.

prompt: An insured accountant loses the sight of both eyes in an accident. His disability policy includes a presumptive disability provision. What happens?

options.text: He must first satisfy a 6-month elimination period
He receives a partial benefit because he can still earn income
He receives benefits only if he cannot do any job
He is considered totally disabled even if he could still work

explanation: Presumptive disability provisions treat specified severe losses (sight, hearing, speech, or use of two limbs) as total disability, paying full benefits even if the insured returns to work.

distractorExplanations.a: Presumptive disability benefits typically begin without the usual elimination period.
distractorExplanations.b: Presumptive disability pays full benefits regardless of earnings.
distractorExplanations.c: Presumptive disability does not depend on an any-occupation test.

prompt: Before disability, Amir earned $10,000 a month. After a heart attack he returns to work part-time earning $4,000 a month. His policy's full benefit is $5,000 a month and includes a residual disability benefit. What does he receive?

options.text: $2,000 a month
$3,000 a month
$5,000 a month
$6,000 a month

explanation: Residual benefits are proportional to income loss: (10,000 − 4,000)/10,000 = 60% loss, so 60% × $5,000 = $3,000 a month.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the 40% of income he still earns instead of the 60% he lost.
distractorExplanations.c: The full benefit is paid only for total disability.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays his income loss in dollars, which exceeds the policy's $5,000 benefit.

prompt: An insured recovers from a disability, returns to work for 3 months, and then becomes disabled again from the same cause. Under a typical recurrent disability provision, what happens?

options.text: It is treated as the same disability, with no new elimination period
Benefits are cut in half for the second period
No benefits are paid, because the cause is pre-existing
It is a new disability, so a new elimination period must be satisfied

explanation: A recurrent disability provision treats a relapse from the same cause within a set period (commonly 6 months) as a continuation of the original disability. No new elimination period applies, and the benefit period continues.

distractorExplanations.b: There is no 50% reduction for recurrent disabilities.
distractorExplanations.c: The earlier disability was covered, so it is not a pre-existing exclusion.
distractorExplanations.d: A recurrence within the stated window, often 6 months, is treated as the same claim.

prompt: A dentist who owns her practice wants coverage for rent, staff salaries, and utilities if she becomes disabled. Which policy fits?

options.text: Key person disability insurance
Disability buy-sell insurance
Business overhead expense insurance
Individual disability income insurance

explanation: Business overhead expense (BOE) insurance reimburses ongoing business expenses such as rent, utilities, and employee salaries while the owner is disabled, usually for 1–2 years. Premiums are deductible and benefits are taxable.

distractorExplanations.a: Key person DI pays the business for lost profits when a key employee is disabled.
distractorExplanations.b: Disability buy-sell funds the purchase of a disabled owner's interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Individual DI replaces her personal income, not business expenses.

prompt: A worker files for Social Security Disability Insurance after a stroke. How long must he generally wait before benefits begin?

options.text: No waiting period at all
A 90-day elimination period
A 12-month waiting period
A 5-month waiting period

explanation: SSDI requires a disability expected to last at least 12 months or result in death, and pays after a 5-month waiting period. Its strict definition is inability to do any substantial gainful work.

distractorExplanations.a: SSDI benefits begin after a full 5-month waiting period.
distractorExplanations.b: Ninety days is a common private DI elimination period, not SSDI's.
distractorExplanations.c: Twelve months is the expected duration of disability, not the waiting period.

prompt: A tax-qualified long-term care policy pays benefits when a licensed health practitioner certifies which condition?

options.text: Inability to do 2 of 6 daily living activities, or severe cognitive impairment
Admission to a hospital for at least 3 consecutive days
Inability to perform the material duties of the insured's own occupation for 90 days
Reaching age 65 with any chronic medical condition

explanation: Tax-qualified LTC policies pay when the insured is chronically ill: unable to perform at least 2 of 6 activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, continence) for 90 days or more, or severely cognitively impaired.

distractorExplanations.b: A prior hospital stay requirement is not allowed in tax-qualified LTC policies.
distractorExplanations.c: Occupation-based definitions apply to disability income insurance, not LTC.
distractorExplanations.d: Age and diagnosis alone do not trigger LTC benefits.

prompt: An LTC insured needs help with bathing and dressing at home from an aide with no medical training. Which level of care is this?

options.text: Intermediate care
Skilled nursing care
Custodial care
Acute hospital care

explanation: Custodial care helps with activities of daily living and can be given by people without medical training. It is the most common type of long-term care and is generally not covered by Medicare.

distractorExplanations.a: Intermediate care is occasional skilled care, such as periodic nursing visits.
distractorExplanations.b: Skilled care is daily care ordered by a physician and given by licensed medical staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Acute hospital care treats short-term illness or injury in a hospital.

prompt: A disability income policy defines 'regular care of a physician.' The insured stops seeing her doctor while claiming total disability. What is the most likely effect?

options.text: The insurer may stop benefits until she is under a physician's care again
The insurer must convert the policy to long-term care coverage
Nothing, because disability benefits do not depend on ongoing medical care
The insurer must double the benefit to cover self-care costs

explanation: Most disability income policies define total disability to include being under the regular care of a physician. Stopping care can let the insurer suspend benefits until the requirement is met again.

distractorExplanations.b: There is no automatic conversion of DI to LTC for this reason.
distractorExplanations.c: Most DI policies require the insured to be under a physician's regular care.
distractorExplanations.d: No provision increases benefits when the insured stops medical care.

prompt: An individual disability policyholder changes jobs from office manager to roofer, a more hazardous occupation, and does not tell the insurer. She later files a claim. What does the change of occupation provision allow?

options.text: Reducing benefits to what her premium would buy at the riskier rate
Voiding the policy and refunding all premiums paid
Paying full benefits, because occupation changes do not affect disability claims
Increasing benefits to reflect the higher-risk job

explanation: Under the change of occupation provision, if the insured moves to a more hazardous occupation, benefits are reduced to what the premium paid would have bought at the higher-risk rate. A safer change may bring a premium refund.

distractorExplanations.b: The provision adjusts benefits; it does not void the policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Occupation is a key rating factor for disability coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: A more hazardous job reduces benefits; a less hazardous one may lower the premium.
